title: Situs and Cardiac Position
front clue: Find fetal left first: stomach, heart apex and aorta all belong on the left
core concept: Every fetal echo begins by establishing fetal right and left from fetal lie and presentation, not from the screen orientation. In the upper abdominal transverse view, normal situs solitus places the stomach on the left, the descending aorta to the left and anterior of the spine, and the inferior vena cava to the right and more anterior. In the chest, the heart lies mostly in the left hemithorax with the apex pointing left (levocardia). Situs inversus is a full mirror image. Situs ambiguus (heterotaxy) is any other arrangement, such as a stomach on one side and the apex on the other, or the aorta and IVC on the same side of the spine. Cardiac position describes where the heart sits: dextroposition is a shift to the right by an external cause such as a left congenital diaphragmatic hernia or a left-sided lung mass, while dextrocardia means the base-to-apex axis itself points right. The heart normally occupies about one third of the thoracic area.
why it matters: Many complex lesions are missed because the sonographer assumes left and right from the image instead of proving them from fetal position. A practical method: identify the fetal head and spine, then work out which side is up. Stomach and heart on opposite sides should immediately raise heterotaxy and send you looking for interrupted IVC, isomerism and complex intracardiac disease. Trap: a heart pushed right by a hernia is dextroposition with a normal axis; dextrocardia is an intrinsic abnormal axis. Keep these terms distinct because answer choices often swap them.
on the registry: Expect items that describe stomach, aorta and IVC positions and ask for the situs, or that distinguish dextroposition caused by a chest mass from true dextrocardia.
checkpoint: Prove fetal left first; stomach, apex and aorta should agree

title: Cardiac Axis
front clue: A line along the septum should sit about 45 degrees left of the midline
core concept: Cardiac axis is the angle between the interventricular septum and the anteroposterior line drawn from the spine to the anterior chest wall in the four-chamber view. The normal axis is about 45 degrees to the left, with a commonly taught normal range of roughly 25 to 65 degrees (45 plus or minus 20). Left axis deviation beyond about 65 degrees is strongly associated with congenital heart disease, especially conotruncal anomalies such as tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus and double outlet right ventricle, and it can also occur with Ebstein anomaly or with extracardiac causes such as diaphragmatic hernia. An axis that is too small (rightward) or that points right is also abnormal. Cardiac size is checked at the same time: the cardiothoracic area ratio is normally about 0.25 to 0.35, and the cardiothoracic circumference ratio about 0.5. Axis is useful early in pregnancy because it can be measured even when chamber detail is limited.
why it matters: The axis is a cheap screening gate: a four-chamber view can look superficially normal in tetralogy of Fallot, but the axis is often shifted left, prompting a closer look at the outflows. Reason from the mechanism: anything that rotates the heart (abnormal outflow development, mass effect, cardiomegaly) changes the angle. Traps include measuring from an oblique plane, which distorts the angle, and confusing axis with position. A normal position with an abnormal axis still needs a full fetal echo, because the angle itself is the warning sign.
on the registry: Questions give an angle (for example 75 degrees) and ask whether it is normal and what lesion class it suggests, or ask for the normal range.
checkpoint: 45 plus or minus 20 degrees; more leftward suggests conotruncal disease

title: Four-Chamber View
front clue: Two atria, two ventricles, a crux and an offset: the core screening plane
core concept: The four-chamber view is a transverse plane of the fetal chest just above the diaphragm. Normal findings: the heart fills about one third of the chest; the apex points left; atria and ventricles are roughly equal in size, with the right ventricle slightly larger late in gestation; the foramen ovale flap moves into the left atrium; at least two pulmonary veins enter the left atrium; and the descending aorta sits left and anterior to the spine. The right ventricle is the most anterior chamber, has a coarse apex and contains the moderator band. The tricuspid valve inserts slightly closer to the apex than the mitral valve, and this normal offset defines the right-sided atrioventricular valve. The crux shows the atrial septum primum, the inlet septum and both AV valves meeting in a cross. Both AV valves should open and close freely, and the septum should be intact from crux to apex.
why it matters: The four-chamber view alone detects only around half of major heart defects, so it is necessary but not sufficient; outflow and three-vessel views must be added. Use it to identify the morphologic right ventricle by the moderator band and the more apical tricuspid valve, not by its position, because chambers can be on the wrong side. Trap: the apical view with the septum parallel to the beam produces false septal dropout near the crux. Trap two: chamber disproportion in the third trimester may be normal, but disproportion before that needs evaluation for coarctation.
on the registry: Expect items on how to identify the morphologic right ventricle, what the normal offset means, and which lesions are typically missed if only the four-chamber view is obtained.
checkpoint: Moderator band plus apical tricuspid insertion equals morphologic RV

title: Outflow Tracts
front clue: Aorta leaves the LV heading right; the PA leaves the RV and crosses over it
core concept: Normal outflows cross. Sliding cranially from the four-chamber view, the left ventricular outflow tract (five-chamber view) shows the aorta arising from the left ventricle and heading toward the fetal right shoulder, with the anterior aortic wall continuous with the interventricular septum and the posterior wall continuous with the anterior mitral leaflet (mitral-aortic fibrous continuity). Further cranial, the right ventricular outflow tract shows the pulmonary artery arising from the anterior right ventricle, crossing in front of the aorta at nearly a right angle, and then bifurcating into right and left pulmonary branches, with the ductus arteriosus continuing toward the descending aorta. The pulmonary valve is normally slightly larger than the aortic valve. Identify each great artery by its branching, not its position: the pulmonary artery bifurcates soon after its origin, while the aorta curves into an arch that gives off head and neck vessels.
why it matters: Parallel great arteries that do not cross are the classic sign of transposition or double outlet right ventricle. A break in septal-aortic continuity with the aorta straddling the septum means override, seen in tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus and some DORV. Reason by branching: the vessel that splits is the pulmonary artery, whatever ventricle it leaves. Trap: an oblique cut can make a normal aorta appear to override the septum, so confirm in more than one plane. Trap two: in truncus there is only one outflow valve.
on the registry: Typical questions describe parallel outflows, override or a vessel that bifurcates from the left ventricle and ask for the diagnosis.
checkpoint: Normal outflows cross; the vessel that branches early is the pulmonary artery

title: Three-Vessel Trachea View
front clue: PA, aorta, SVC left to right, shrinking in size, with a V left of trachea
core concept: The three-vessel and three-vessel trachea views are transverse planes of the upper mediastinum above the four-chamber view. In the three-vessel view, from fetal left anterior to right posterior, are the main pulmonary artery, the ascending aorta and the superior vena cava, arranged in a nearly straight line and decreasing in size (PA larger than aorta larger than SVC). Slightly more cranially, the three-vessel trachea view shows the ductal arch and the transverse aortic arch joining in a V shape to the left of the trachea, with both flowing in the same direction (same color) toward the descending aorta. Abnormal findings include a vessel count other than three (a persistent left SVC adds a vessel left of the PA), abnormal size relationships, abnormal alignment, a right aortic arch passing to the right of the trachea, a U-shaped vascular ring around the trachea, and reversed flow in one arch. The thymus lies anterior to the vessels.
why it matters: This plane is high-yield because it detects lesions the four-chamber view misses: transposition (one large anterior vessel), tetralogy (large aorta, small PA), coarctation (small arch), and arch anomalies. Color flow direction is the key reasoning tool: reversed flow in the transverse arch means systemic circulation depends on the ductus (HLHS, critical AS), while reversed ductal flow means the pulmonary circulation depends on the aorta (pulmonary atresia). Trap: a right arch with left ductus forms a vascular ring that may compress the trachea and esophagus after birth.
on the registry: Expect questions on the normal order and size of vessels, what a fourth vessel represents, and what reversed arch or ductal flow implies.
checkpoint: PA bigger than Ao bigger than SVC, V to the left of the trachea, same color

title: Aortic and Ductal Arches
front clue: Candy cane with three branches versus a flat hockey stick with none
core concept: Sagittal views show the two arches that both reach the descending aorta. The aortic arch has a tight, rounded candy-cane shape arising centrally from the heart and gives off three head and neck vessels (brachiocephalic, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries). The ductal arch is broader and flatter, often described as a hockey stick, arising more anteriorly from the right ventricle via the pulmonary artery and ductus arteriosus, with no head and neck branches. The isthmus, between the left subclavian artery and the ductal insertion, is normally slightly narrower than the transverse arch in the fetus. The bicaval view, a parasagittal plane to the right, shows the superior and inferior vena cavae entering the right atrium, with the Eustachian valve at the IVC orifice. Pulsed Doppler of the ductus arteriosus normally shows forward flow toward the descending aorta throughout the cycle, with systolic velocity rising with gestational age.
why it matters: Arch views confirm what the three-vessel trachea view suggests. A long, narrow isthmus or posterior shelf supports coarctation; a missing segment suggests interruption, which is strongly linked to 22q11 deletion. Ductal constriction (high systolic and diastolic velocity, reduced pulsatility) occurs with maternal NSAID use in the third trimester. Trap: the two arches can look alike in a single sagittal plane, so prove the aortic arch by its head and neck branches. Trap two: an absent IVC segment in the bicaval view points to interrupted IVC with azygos continuation.
on the registry: Questions ask which arch has branches, what the normal ductal Doppler looks like, and which drug causes ductal constriction.
checkpoint: Aortic arch candy cane gives branches; ductal arch hockey stick gives none

title: Fetal Shunts
front clue: Ductus venosus, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus: three bypasses around liver and lungs
core concept: The placenta, not the lungs, oxygenates fetal blood. Oxygenated blood returns in the umbilical vein. The ductus venosus, a narrow trumpet-shaped vessel from the umbilical vein to the IVC near the right atrium, shunts part of this blood past the liver (roughly a quarter to a third at midgestation, less near term). Its high-velocity stream is directed by the Eustachian valve and the crista dividens across the foramen ovale into the left atrium, so the best-oxygenated blood reaches the left ventricle, coronary arteries and brain. Deoxygenated blood from the SVC is directed mainly through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. Because pulmonary vascular resistance is high, most right ventricular output crosses the ductus arteriosus to the descending aorta and returns to the placenta via the umbilical arteries. The fetal ventricles work in parallel, and the right ventricle carries slightly more than half of combined cardiac output.
why it matters: Thinking of the circulation as parallel explains several exam points: a fetus with HLHS or pulmonary atresia can thrive in utero because the other ventricle and the shunts take over, then decompensate when the ducts close after birth. Normal foramen ovale flow is right to left; left-to-right flow signals left heart obstruction. Trap: the ductus venosus carries oxygenated blood, not deoxygenated. Trap two: the umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the placenta, the reverse of the adult naming logic.
on the registry: Expect items on which shunt bypasses which organ, the direction of normal foramen ovale flow, and which ventricle is dominant in the fetus.
checkpoint: DV bypasses liver, FO and DA bypass lungs; RV is the dominant fetal ventricle

title: Ductus Venosus Doppler
front clue: Always forward: S, D and an a-wave that should stay above the baseline
core concept: The ductus venosus is found in a midsagittal or oblique transverse plane of the upper abdomen, where color Doppler shows aliasing at its narrow inlet from the umbilical vein. The sample volume is placed at the inlet with a small angle. The normal waveform is triphasic and entirely forward: a peak during ventricular systole (S wave), a second peak during early diastole (D wave), and a nadir during atrial contraction (a-wave) that remains forward. Peak velocities are much higher than in the umbilical vein, commonly 50 to 80 cm/s in the second half of pregnancy. Pulsatility index for veins is calculated as (S minus a) divided by time-averaged maximum velocity. An absent or reversed a-wave is abnormal and reflects raised right atrial pressure or poor ventricular compliance. In the first trimester, reversed a-wave is a marker for aneuploidy and congenital heart disease. Later, it signals cardiac failure or advanced decompensation in growth restriction.
why it matters: DV is the venous window into right heart pressure. In growth restriction, the sequence typically runs from abnormal umbilical artery to brain sparing to abnormal DV, and reversed a-wave is a late, ominous finding that often guides delivery timing. Trap: sampling the adjacent hepatic vein or umbilical vein contaminates the signal and can create a false reversed a-wave, so confirm aliasing at the DV inlet and use a small sample volume. Pulsations in the umbilical vein itself are another sign of elevated venous pressure.
on the registry: Questions describe a waveform with an a-wave below baseline and ask what it means, or ask where to place the sample gate.
checkpoint: Reversed a-wave in the DV means high right atrial pressure

title: Umbilical Artery Doppler
front clue: Low-resistance placenta: diastolic flow should rise as pregnancy advances
core concept: The umbilical artery reflects downstream placental resistance. Normally, as the placental vascular bed expands, end-diastolic flow increases and resistance indices (pulsatility index, resistance index and S/D ratio) fall steadily with gestational age. Sampling a free loop of cord gives the most reproducible values; values are higher near the fetal insertion and lower near the placental insertion. Measurements are taken without fetal breathing or movement, with a small angle of insonation, and compared against gestational age reference ranges. Abnormal findings progress through elevated PI, absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) and then reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF), reflecting increasing loss of functioning placental villous vessels. A single umbilical artery is a separate finding associated with cardiac and renal anomalies and is often confirmed with color Doppler around the fetal bladder.
why it matters: Umbilical artery Doppler tells you about the placenta, not the heart, but fetal echo labs use it to judge whether an abnormal heart is also under placental stress. AEDF and REDF in a growth-restricted fetus mean high risk and closer surveillance or delivery. Trap: a high-resistance waveform early in pregnancy can be normal, because end-diastolic flow is often absent in the first trimester. Trap two: fetal breathing changes the waveform, so a single abnormal trace during breathing should be repeated.
on the registry: Expect questions on the normal trend of UA indices with gestational age and the significance of AEDF and REDF.
checkpoint: UA resistance falls as pregnancy advances; AEDF then REDF means placental failure

title: Middle Cerebral Artery Doppler
front clue: Zero degrees near the circle of Willis: PSV for anemia, PI for brain sparing
core concept: The middle cerebral artery is imaged in an axial view of the fetal head at the level of the circle of Willis, using color Doppler. The sample volume is placed in the proximal third of the MCA, close to its origin, with an angle of insonation as close to zero as possible (angle correction kept minimal). The normal MCA waveform is high resistance with low diastolic flow. Peak systolic velocity (PSV) increases with gestational age and rises in fetal anemia because of lower blood viscosity and higher cardiac output; a value above 1.5 multiples of the median (MoM) suggests moderate to severe anemia, as in red cell alloimmunization or parvovirus infection. In placental insufficiency, cerebral vasodilation lowers the MCA PI (brain sparing). The cerebroplacental ratio (MCA PI divided by UA PI) falls when this redistribution occurs; a value below about 1, or below the 5th percentile, is abnormal.
why it matters: MCA PSV replaced invasive amniocentesis for anemia screening, so the technique details are high yield: proximal segment, near-zero angle, fetus at rest, no excessive transducer pressure on the head. Fetal anemia is a high-output cause of hydrops, so it belongs in the fetal echo differential for cardiomegaly. Trap: brain sparing lowers the MCA PI but does not mean the fetus is healthy; it signals adaptation to hypoxemia. Trap two: sampling the distal MCA underestimates PSV.
on the registry: Questions ask for the anemia cutoff (1.5 MoM), correct sampling location and angle, or the meaning of a low cerebroplacental ratio.
checkpoint: MCA PSV above 1.5 MoM equals anemia; low MCA PI equals brain sparing

title: Atrioventricular Valve Inflow Doppler
front clue: Fetal inflow is A-dominant: E smaller than A, two separate peaks at normal heart rates
core concept: Pulsed Doppler with the sample volume just distal to the mitral or tricuspid valve leaflets, in an apical four-chamber view with the beam parallel to flow, shows a biphasic inflow pattern. The E wave reflects early passive ventricular filling and the A wave reflects atrial contraction. Because fetal myocardium is relatively stiff, the A wave is taller than the E wave, giving an E/A ratio below 1 that gradually rises toward 1 as gestation advances. A monophasic inflow (fused E and A, or a single peak) suggests diastolic dysfunction or a very fast heart rate, and is seen for example in the recipient twin of twin-twin transfusion syndrome. Color and pulsed Doppler also screen for AV valve regurgitation, which should be timed and measured; mild, brief tricuspid regurgitation is common and often trivial, while holosystolic regurgitation with high velocity is significant. Outflow velocities across semilunar valves normally rise with gestational age and generally remain below about 1 m/s in midgestation.
why it matters: Inflow Doppler is the simplest bedside test of diastolic function. Reason from physiology: a stiff ventricle relies on the atrial kick, which is why the A wave dominates. Trap: at high heart rates E and A merge even in a normal heart, so check the rate before calling a monophasic pattern abnormal. Trap two: tricuspid regurgitation in the first trimester is an aneuploidy marker, while a little early-systolic TR later may be normal.
on the registry: Expect items on the normal fetal E/A ratio (less than 1), the meaning of monophasic inflow, and correct sample volume placement.
checkpoint: Fetal E/A is below 1; monophasic inflow suggests diastolic dysfunction

title: Transitional Circulation
front clue: First breath drops lung resistance; ducts close and parallel becomes series
core concept: At birth, lung expansion and oxygen sharply lower pulmonary vascular resistance, so pulmonary blood flow and left atrial return increase. Removal of the low-resistance placenta raises systemic vascular resistance. Left atrial pressure now exceeds right atrial pressure, pressing the foramen ovale flap against the septum and closing it functionally. The ductus arteriosus constricts in response to the rise in oxygen and the fall in circulating prostaglandins, usually closing functionally within the first one to three days; it becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. The ductus venosus closes once umbilical venous flow stops and becomes the ligamentum venosum. The circulation changes from two ventricles pumping in parallel to two ventricles in series. Lesions that rely on the ductus are called ductal dependent: systemic flow (HLHS, critical coarctation, critical aortic stenosis), pulmonary flow (pulmonary atresia, critical pulmonary stenosis, tricuspid atresia with pulmonary obstruction) or mixing (transposition with intact septum). Prostaglandin E1 infusion keeps the ductus open.
why it matters: This card explains why prenatal diagnosis saves lives: a ductal-dependent baby may look well at delivery and collapse within days as the duct closes. Fetal echo identifies which lesions need delivery at a cardiac center with prostaglandin ready. Reason by asking what the closing duct removes. Trap: transposition depends on mixing at the atrial level as much as at the duct, so a restrictive foramen ovale in d-TGA requires urgent balloon atrial septostomy after birth.
on the registry: Questions ask what closes the foramen ovale, what keeps the ductus open, and which lesions are ductal dependent for systemic or pulmonary flow.
checkpoint: Duct closes, ductal-dependent baby crashes; prostaglandin E1 keeps it open

title: Ventricular Septal Defects
front clue: Hole in the septum with quiet bidirectional flow, because fetal pressures are equal
core concept: A ventricular septal defect is the most common congenital heart defect after bicuspid aortic valve. Types are named by location: perimembranous (the most common postnatally, just below the aortic valve near the tricuspid septal leaflet), muscular (trabecular, in the apical or mid septum, often small and multiple), inlet (posterior, at the level of the AV valves, typical of AV septal defect) and outlet (subarterial or malalignment, beneath the great arteries, typical of conotruncal lesions). Best seen with the septum perpendicular to the beam, using a subcostal or lateral four-chamber view and the five-chamber view, the defect appears as a gap with blunt, slightly echogenic edges. Because right and left ventricular pressures are nearly equal in the fetus, color Doppler shows low-velocity, often bidirectional flow, so lowering the color scale helps. Small muscular defects frequently close spontaneously before or after birth, while malalignment defects signal possible tetralogy, DORV or truncus.
why it matters: The biggest trap is septal dropout: when the beam is parallel to the thin membranous septum, a false gap appears near the crux. Confirm a defect in two planes with the beam perpendicular and with color flow across it. Reason about flow: no pressure gradient in utero means no high-velocity jet, so a loud jet is not expected. An isolated small muscular VSD has a good prognosis, but an outlet or malalignment VSD should trigger a careful search for override and outflow obstruction.
on the registry: Expect questions on VSD types and locations, the cause of false septal dropout, and why fetal VSD flow is low velocity and bidirectional.
checkpoint: Perpendicular beam, two planes, low color scale: then call the VSD

title: Atrial Septal Defects
front clue: The foramen ovale should be open; look for a missing primum or abnormal flap instead
core concept: Because the foramen ovale is a normal opening, a secundum atrial septal defect generally cannot be diagnosed reliably before birth. Suspicion arises only when the foramen appears unusually large relative to the septum or the flap is absent. The ostium primum defect, a gap in the lower atrial septum just above the AV valves, is diagnosable and represents the partial form of atrioventricular septal defect, usually with a cleft mitral valve and two separate AV valve orifices on a common annulus. Sinus venosus defects lie near the SVC or IVC entry and are often associated with anomalous right pulmonary venous return; they are rarely seen prenatally. Abnormalities of the flap itself are important: a redundant or aneurysmal flap bulging into the left atrium is associated with premature atrial contractions, and a restrictive or prematurely closed foramen ovale can cause right heart dilation and, in left heart obstruction, severe left atrial hypertension.
why it matters: Think of the atrial septum in the fetus as a valve, not a wall: it must let blood pass right to left. A question that asks you to diagnose a secundum ASD prenatally is usually testing whether you know it is not reliably possible. Trap: mistaking the normal foramen ovale for a defect. Trap two: missing a primum defect because the AV valves look separate; check whether the lowest portion of the atrial septum is present and whether the normal offset is preserved.
on the registry: Questions ask which ASD type is detectable prenatally, what a primum defect implies, and what a restrictive foramen ovale does to the heart.
checkpoint: Secundum ASD is a postnatal diagnosis; primum ASD equals partial AVSD

title: Atrioventricular Septal Defect
front clue: One common valve at the crux; no offset; think trisomy 21
core concept: Atrioventricular septal defect (AV canal, endocardial cushion defect) results from failed development of the endocardial cushions. In the complete form there is a primum atrial defect, an inlet ventricular defect and a single common AV valve, so the crux of the heart is missing. In the four-chamber view the normal offset is lost: both AV valve components insert at the same level, creating a linear insertion. In systole the common valve appears as a straight line across the heart, and in diastole the valve opens to show a large central defect. Color Doppler often shows a single inflow stream and AV valve regurgitation. In the partial form, a primum ASD and cleft mitral valve exist with two orifices. AVSD is balanced when both ventricles are adequately sized or unbalanced when one is hypoplastic. About 40 to 50 percent of fetuses with AVSD have trisomy 21, and AVSD is also common in heterotaxy, particularly right atrial isomerism.
why it matters: AVSD is the classic heart defect of Down syndrome, so a fetal AVSD should prompt genetic counseling and offer of diagnostic testing. Unbalanced AVSD with heterotaxy has a much worse prognosis and different genetics. Trap: the inlet VSD may be small and the defect can be missed if you look only in systole; watch the crux through the cardiac cycle. Significant AV valve regurgitation, hydrops or associated heart block worsens outcome.
on the registry: Expect items that describe a linear AV valve insertion with a central defect and ask for the diagnosis or the most likely associated chromosomal abnormality.
checkpoint: No offset, no crux, common valve: AVSD, think trisomy 21

title: Trisomy 21 and the Fetal Heart
front clue: About half of trisomy 21 fetuses have heart disease, led by AVSD and VSD
core concept: Congenital heart disease occurs in roughly 40 to 50 percent of individuals with trisomy 21. Atrioventricular septal defect is the most characteristic lesion and accounts for a large share, followed by ventricular septal defect, tetralogy of Fallot and patent ductus arteriosus. Transposition and left-sided obstructive lesions are uncommon in Down syndrome. In the first trimester, cardiac-related markers include increased nuchal translucency, tricuspid regurgitation and a reversed a-wave in the ductus venosus. In the second trimester, soft markers include an echogenic intracardiac focus and an aberrant right subclavian artery (ARSA), which arises from the descending aorta as the last arch branch and passes behind the trachea to the right, seen on color Doppler in the three-vessel trachea view. These soft markers carry only a small increase in risk when isolated. A detected cardiac defect, by contrast, significantly raises the risk and changes counseling.
why it matters: Know the hierarchy: a structural defect such as AVSD is a major marker, while an isolated EIF or ARSA is a weak soft marker whose significance depends on prior risk and cell-free DNA results. Reason by lesion family: cushion defects point to trisomy 21; conotruncal lesions point toward 22q11 deletion; left-sided obstruction points toward Turner syndrome. Trap: do not assume trisomy 21 for every VSD; isolated small muscular VSDs are common in chromosomally normal fetuses.
on the registry: Questions ask which heart defect is most characteristic of trisomy 21 and how to weigh soft markers such as EIF or ARSA.
checkpoint: Cushions mean Down syndrome; conotruncal means 22q11; left obstruction means Turner

title: Echogenic Intracardiac Focus
front clue: A bone-bright dot in the left ventricle that moves with the papillary muscle
core concept: An echogenic intracardiac focus (EIF) is a small, bright echo within a ventricle, most often the left, as bright as bone at the same gain, located at the level of the papillary muscle or chordae and moving with the AV valve apparatus. It represents microcalcification or fibrosis of the papillary muscle and is not a structural defect. EIF is seen in a few percent of normal second-trimester fetuses, and it is more common in people of Asian ancestry. It is classified as a soft marker for trisomy 21, but when isolated in a low-risk pregnancy with normal screening it has little clinical significance and does not change heart function. Multiple, right-sided or biventricular foci carry slightly more concern for aneuploidy, particularly trisomy 13. To call an EIF, reduce gain and confirm the focus remains as bright as adjacent rib or spine. Distinguish it from a rhabdomyoma, which is a larger, homogeneous, non-shadowing mass that grows.
why it matters: EIF tests whether you can avoid overcalling. The right response is to place it in context of other markers and screening results rather than to alarm the parent or label the heart abnormal. Trap: brightness from high gain or harmonics can mimic EIF; reduce gain to confirm. Trap two: a growing echogenic mass in the septum or ventricle is not an EIF but suggests rhabdomyoma, which carries a very different association with tuberous sclerosis.
on the registry: Expect items asking what an EIF represents, its usual location, and its significance when isolated in a low-risk pregnancy.
checkpoint: Isolated EIF in a low-risk pregnancy is a normal variant

title: Tetralogy of Fallot
front clue: Big overriding aorta, small pulmonary artery, malalignment VSD; four chambers may look normal
core concept: Tetralogy of Fallot results from anterior and cephalad deviation of the outlet septum. The four classic components are a malalignment ventricular septal defect, an aorta that overrides the septum, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction (infundibular and valvar pulmonary stenosis) and right ventricular hypertrophy. Right ventricular hypertrophy usually develops after birth and is rarely seen in the fetus. The four-chamber view is often normal, though the axis may be shifted to the left. The five-chamber view shows a large aorta straddling a subaortic VSD, with loss of continuity between the septum and the anterior aortic wall. The pulmonary artery is smaller than the aorta, reversing the normal size relationship in the three-vessel view. Color Doppler shows both ventricles ejecting into the aorta, and the pulmonary flow may be accelerated. Reversed flow in the ductus indicates severe obstruction or pulmonary atresia with ductal-dependent pulmonary flow. A right aortic arch occurs in about a quarter of cases.
why it matters: Tetralogy is a key reason the outflow views are part of screening. Assess the pulmonary artery size and ductal flow direction serially, because obstruction often progresses during pregnancy. Associations matter: 22q11 deletion (particularly with right arch, pulmonary atresia or absent thymus), trisomy 21 and maternal diabetes. Trap: override alone also occurs in truncus arteriosus and DORV; tetralogy has a separate, small pulmonary artery arising from the right ventricle and more than half of the aorta over the left ventricle.
on the registry: Expect questions listing override plus a small PA and asking for the diagnosis, which component is rarely seen prenatally, or what reversed ductal flow implies.
checkpoint: Override plus small PA equals tetralogy; RVH appears after birth

title: Absent Pulmonary Valve Syndrome
front clue: Huge pulsating pulmonary arteries with to-and-fro flow; no valve, no ductus
core concept: Absent pulmonary valve syndrome is usually a variant of tetralogy of Fallot in which the pulmonary valve leaflets are rudimentary or absent. The valve ring is narrow, so flow is both obstructed and freely regurgitant, producing a to-and-fro color and spectral Doppler pattern across the annulus, with high forward velocity and holodiastolic regurgitation. The main and branch pulmonary arteries become massively dilated and pulsatile, seen as large fluid-filled structures in the upper mediastinum. The ductus arteriosus is typically absent. A malalignment VSD with an overriding aorta is present, as in tetralogy. The enlarged pulmonary arteries can compress the trachea and bronchi, causing bronchomalacia and serious respiratory compromise after birth. Volume overload of the right ventricle can lead to cardiomegaly and hydrops. Absent pulmonary valve syndrome has a strong association with 22q11 deletion.
why it matters: The reasoning link is the missing ductus: in normal fetal life the ductus decompresses the pulmonary trunk, and without it the regurgitant volume dilates the pulmonary arteries. Trap: a cystic structure in the upper chest that fills with color is vascular, not a bronchogenic cyst. Trap two: the pulmonary artery is large, not small, so do not rule out tetralogy because the PA is dilated. Prognosis is driven largely by airway compression, not the heart repair alone.
on the registry: Questions describe dilated pulmonary arteries with to-and-fro flow and ask for the diagnosis or its major postnatal complication.
checkpoint: To-and-fro pulmonary flow plus aneurysmal PAs equals absent pulmonary valve

title: D-Transposition of the Great Arteries
front clue: Parallel outflows: aorta from the RV, branching PA from the LV
core concept: In d-transposition of the great arteries (d-TGA), the atria and ventricles connect normally (atrioventricular concordance) but the great arteries are switched (ventriculoarterial discordance). The aorta arises from the right ventricle, usually anterior and to the right, and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle, posterior. Because the outflows do not cross, they run parallel in the long-axis view. The vessel arising from the left ventricle bifurcates early, proving it is the pulmonary artery. The four-chamber view is usually normal, which is why d-TGA is frequently missed on screening. In the three-vessel trachea view, typically only two vessels are seen, a large transverse aortic arch and the SVC, because the pulmonary artery lies lower. d-TGA may be simple, with intact septum, or complex with a VSD or pulmonary stenosis. There is a male predominance and a low rate of chromosomal abnormalities or extracardiac anomalies, although maternal diabetes is a risk factor.
why it matters: After birth, the two circulations run in parallel, so survival depends on mixing at the foramen ovale and ductus. A restrictive or hypermobile foramen ovale flap or a small ductus in utero predicts severe neonatal hypoxemia needing urgent balloon atrial septostomy, so delivery should occur at a cardiac surgical center. Definitive repair is the arterial switch. Trap: a normal four-chamber view with normal axis does not exclude TGA. Trap two: unlike conotruncal lesions such as truncus, TGA has a weak link to 22q11 deletion.
on the registry: Expect a scenario of parallel great arteries with a normal four-chamber view, and questions on the vessel identification, postnatal emergency or repair.
checkpoint: Normal four chambers, parallel outflows, PA from the LV: d-TGA
ai_review_note: whyLock (low): 'Unlike conotruncal lesions' implies TGA is not conotruncal, which contradicts the 22q11/Turner card that classes TGA as a conotruncal lesion with a low 22q11 rate.

title: Congenitally Corrected Transposition
front clue: Double discordance: wrong ventricle, wrong artery, so blood ends up in the right place
core concept: Congenitally corrected transposition (ccTGA, l-TGA) has both atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance. The right atrium connects through a mitral valve to a morphologic left ventricle, which gives rise to the pulmonary artery; the left atrium connects through a tricuspid valve to a morphologic right ventricle, which gives rise to the aorta. Blood is therefore physiologically routed correctly, but the morphologic right ventricle serves as the systemic ventricle. In the four-chamber view the clue is that the moderator band and the more apically inserted AV valve are in the left-sided ventricle, posterior and left, while the smooth-walled ventricle with the higher AV valve insertion is on the right. The great arteries run parallel, with the aorta usually anterior and to the left. Common associations are VSD, pulmonary stenosis, Ebstein-like abnormality of the left-sided tricuspid valve and congenital heart block, which may be present prenatally or develop progressively.
why it matters: ccTGA is the classic exercise in morphologic chamber identification: you must name each ventricle by its features rather than its position. If a fetus has heart block without maternal antibodies, structural causes such as ccTGA and left atrial isomerism should be sought. Long term, the systemic right ventricle and tricuspid valve may fail. Trap: calling this a normal heart because blood flows in the right sequence; the inverted ventricles and parallel arteries are the tell.
on the registry: Expect questions on the double discordance, how to identify the morphologic right ventricle on the left, and the association with heart block.
checkpoint: Moderator band on the left plus parallel arteries equals ccTGA

title: Truncus Arteriosus
front clue: One great artery, one valve, giving off coronaries, pulmonaries and the aorta
core concept: Truncus arteriosus is a single arterial trunk arising from the heart above a large outlet VSD, with a single semilunar (truncal) valve. The trunk gives rise to the coronary arteries, the pulmonary arteries and the systemic circulation. Classification describes how the pulmonary arteries arise: in the most common form a short main pulmonary segment arises from the trunk and then divides; in other forms the right and left pulmonary arteries arise separately from the posterior or lateral trunk. The four-chamber view is often normal, while the outflow view shows a single large vessel overriding the septum. No separate pulmonary valve or right ventricular outflow is found. The truncal valve may have two to five cusps and is often thickened, stenotic or regurgitant, best assessed with color and spectral Doppler. A right aortic arch or interrupted aortic arch may coexist. Truncus has a strong association with 22q11 deletion, in roughly a third of cases.
why it matters: The key differential is pulmonary atresia with VSD (tetralogy with pulmonary atresia), which also shows a single large overriding vessel; there the pulmonary arteries are supplied by the ductus or collateral arteries, not from the root of the trunk. Following the pulmonary branches back to their origin is the deciding step. Truncal valve regurgitation and arch interruption worsen prognosis. Trap: the large single trunk can mimic tetralogy override, but tetralogy has a separate pulmonary valve arising from the right ventricle.
on the registry: Questions describe a single overriding vessel giving rise to the pulmonary arteries and ask for the diagnosis, the valve abnormality or the genetic association.
checkpoint: Single trunk gives pulmonaries from its root: truncus, think 22q11

title: Double Outlet Right Ventricle
front clue: Both great arteries mostly from the RV; the VSD is the only LV exit
core concept: Double outlet right ventricle (DORV) is a ventriculoarterial connection in which both great arteries arise entirely or predominantly from the right ventricle; the commonly used fifty percent rule assigns an artery to the ventricle that supports more than half of it. The VSD is the only outlet for the left ventricle. The great arteries are often side by side and parallel rather than crossing. DORV is a spectrum defined by the VSD location: a subaortic VSD with pulmonary stenosis behaves like tetralogy of Fallot, a subpulmonary VSD (Taussig-Bing type) behaves like transposition, and a doubly committed or remote VSD complicates repair. Pulmonary stenosis, coarctation and AV valve anomalies frequently coexist. The four-chamber view may be normal. DORV is associated with chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 13 and 18, 22q11 deletion, heterotaxy and maternal diabetes, so extracardiac and genetic evaluation is important.
why it matters: DORV is best reasoned as tetralogy or transposition physiology depending on where the VSD sits relative to the arteries. On the exam, the clue is two great arteries both arising from the anterior ventricle, often parallel, with the left ventricle emptying only through the VSD. Trap: in tetralogy the aorta sits more over the left ventricle, while in DORV the aorta sits mainly over the right ventricle. In practice the distinction can be difficult prenatally and may be refined after birth.
on the registry: Expect a description of both great arteries arising from the right ventricle and questions on the defining rule, subtypes or associations.
checkpoint: Both arteries from the RV, VSD is the LV exit; VSD position decides physiology

title: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome
front clue: Tiny or absent LV, retrograde arch flow, left-to-right flow across the foramen
core concept: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) is underdevelopment of the left heart with mitral and aortic stenosis or atresia and a hypoplastic ascending aorta and arch. The four-chamber view is markedly abnormal: the left ventricle is small or slit-like and fails to reach the apex, or in some forms is globular with an echogenic endocardium from endocardial fibroelastosis. The right ventricle forms the apex and is dilated. Color Doppler shows little or no mitral inflow and flow across the foramen ovale reversed to left-to-right. The ascending aorta is tiny, and in the three-vessel trachea view the transverse arch is small with retrograde (reversed) flow filled from the ductus. The systemic circulation is ductal dependent. Assessment of the atrial septum is critical: a restrictive or intact septum causes pulmonary venous hypertension, seen as prominent reversed flow in pulmonary vein Doppler, and predicts severe neonatal hypoxemia needing urgent intervention.
why it matters: HLHS is usually well tolerated in utero because the right ventricle supports both circulations through the ductus, but it is fatal without treatment after the duct closes. Planned delivery at a cardiac center, prostaglandin E1 and staged palliation (Norwood, then Glenn and Fontan) or transplant are the pathway. Turner syndrome is a recognized association. Trap: a small left ventricle late in pregnancy can also reflect coarctation or a restrictive foramen ovale, so check arch flow direction and AV valve flow before labeling HLHS.
on the registry: Expect items describing a slit-like LV and reversed arch flow, and questions on the direction of foramen ovale flow or the significance of an intact atrial septum.
checkpoint: Small LV, reversed arch flow, left-to-right FO flow equals HLHS

title: Coarctation of the Aorta
front clue: The most missed lesion: RV and PA larger than LV and aorta, narrow isthmus
core concept: Coarctation of the aorta is narrowing of the aortic arch, usually at the isthmus near the ductal insertion. It is among the most difficult major lesions to diagnose prenatally because the ductus carries much of the descending aortic flow in utero. The main clue is ventricular and great artery disproportion, with the right ventricle and pulmonary artery larger than the left ventricle and aorta, especially when seen before the third trimester. Supporting findings include a hypoplastic transverse arch or isthmus on the three-vessel trachea and sagittal arch views, a posterior shelf, an increased distance between the left carotid and left subclavian arteries, continuous high-velocity flow or color aliasing at the isthmus, and left-to-right flow at the foramen ovale. Measurements of the isthmus and transverse arch compared with gestational age (z-scores) improve accuracy. Associations include bicuspid aortic valve, VSD, persistent left SVC and Turner syndrome. Findings frequently produce false positives, so postnatal echo is required.
why it matters: Coarctation tests probability reasoning: prenatal diagnosis is a risk statement, not a certainty, and many suspected cases prove normal after birth. Counseling should emphasize monitored delivery with echo before the ductus closes. Trap: ventricular disproportion alone has many causes, such as a persistent left SVC, a restrictive foramen ovale or normal late-gestation right dominance. Trap two: a dilated coronary sinus behind the left atrium may be a persistent left SVC, which can cause disproportion itself and is associated with coarctation.
on the registry: Expect questions on the key sign of coarctation (ventricular disproportion), the classic genetic association (Turner syndrome) and why prenatal diagnosis is uncertain.
checkpoint: Right-dominant disproportion plus a narrow isthmus suggests coarctation

title: Critical Aortic Stenosis
front clue: A dilated, echogenic, poorly squeezing LV with a narrow jet: watch it evolve
core concept: Aortic stenosis in the fetus is usually valvar, with thickened, doming leaflets and a narrow color jet across the aortic valve showing aliasing and turbulence beyond. Mild stenosis may show only increased peak velocity (above about 1 m/s in midgestation is suspicious) and post-stenotic ascending aortic dilation. In critical aortic stenosis the left ventricle is often dilated and globular with poor contraction, an echogenic endocardium from endocardial fibroelastosis, mitral regurgitation and a dilated left atrium. Because LV function is poor, the measured aortic velocity can be falsely low despite severe obstruction. Flow across the foramen ovale reverses to left-to-right, mitral inflow becomes monophasic and short, and flow in the transverse arch may be retrograde. Midgestation critical aortic stenosis can progress to hypoplastic left heart syndrome as the left ventricle stops growing. Selected fetuses may be candidates for fetal aortic balloon valvuloplasty to try to preserve a two-ventricle circulation.
why it matters: The trap here is relying on velocity: a failing ventricle cannot generate a high gradient, so a low velocity does not exclude critical stenosis. Look instead at LV size, function, endocardial brightness and flow direction in the arch and foramen ovale. Serial scans matter because the lesion evolves. Reason by physiology: rising LV pressure dilates the left atrium and reverses atrial shunting, and when systemic output falls, the ductus fills the arch backwards.
on the registry: Expect questions describing a dilated, echogenic LV with mitral regurgitation and reversed foramen flow, or asking why the aortic velocity may be low.
checkpoint: Failing LV makes velocity lie; judge critical AS by size, function and flow direction

title: Pulmonary Atresia with Intact Septum
front clue: No forward pulmonary flow; the ductus fills the PA backwards; check for sinusoids
core concept: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum (PA/IVS) is an imperforate pulmonary valve without a VSD. The right ventricle is usually small and hypertrophied, with a small tricuspid valve, although some forms have a dilated right ventricle with severe tricuspid regurgitation. No forward flow crosses the pulmonary valve, and color Doppler in the three-vessel or ductal view shows reversed flow in the ductus arteriosus filling the main pulmonary artery from the aorta, so pulmonary blood flow is ductal dependent. The high right ventricular pressure produces a high-velocity tricuspid regurgitation jet when regurgitation is present. Coronary artery fistulas or sinusoids connecting the hypertensive RV cavity to the coronary arteries may be seen with color Doppler, and RV-dependent coronary circulation affects surgical options. Pulmonary valve stenosis, the milder relative, shows a thickened doming valve, high-velocity jet and post-stenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery, and can progress to atresia during pregnancy.
why it matters: Tricuspid valve size (z-score) and RV size predict whether a two-ventricle repair is possible or a single-ventricle pathway is needed. Reasoning link: if the RV cannot eject, all systemic venous return must cross the foramen ovale right to left, and the lungs depend on reversed ductal flow. Trap: pulmonary atresia with a VSD is a different lesion in the tetralogy family. Trap two: the recipient twin in twin-twin transfusion can acquire right outflow obstruction.
on the registry: Questions describe reversed ductal flow with a small hypertrophied RV and ask for the diagnosis or for the finding that limits surgical options.
checkpoint: Reversed ductal flow into the PA means pulmonary flow is ductal dependent

title: Tricuspid Atresia
front clue: No right AV connection: a bright plate where the tricuspid should open
core concept: Tricuspid atresia is absence of the right atrioventricular connection. In the four-chamber view an echogenic, immobile band or plate of tissue sits in place of the tricuspid valve, and color Doppler shows no inflow from the right atrium into the right ventricle. All systemic venous return crosses the foramen ovale right to left into the left atrium, so the foramen must be unrestrictive, and the left ventricle and mitral valve are large. The right ventricle is hypoplastic and filled only through a VSD. Classification depends on great artery relationships: most commonly the arteries are normally related, often with a restrictive VSD or pulmonary stenosis that limits pulmonary flow; less commonly the arteries are transposed, with a risk of systemic outflow obstruction and coarctation. Because the right ventricle is unusable as a pumping chamber, management follows a single-ventricle pathway ending in a Fontan circulation, with early ductal or shunt support if pulmonary flow is inadequate.
why it matters: Tricuspid atresia contrasts with HLHS: here the right side is hypoplastic and the left side large. The flow logic is simple: blood that cannot enter the right ventricle must cross the atrial septum, so a restrictive foramen ovale would be catastrophic. Trap: severe tricuspid stenosis or PA/IVS with a tiny RV can look similar; confirm whether any color inflow crosses the right AV junction. Trap two: VSD size and pulmonary stenosis decide whether the neonate needs prostaglandin.
on the registry: Expect items describing an echogenic plate at the tricuspid position with a large LV and asking for the diagnosis or the eventual surgical pathway.
checkpoint: No tricuspid inflow, big LV, small RV fed by a VSD: tricuspid atresia

title: Ebstein Anomaly
front clue: Septal leaflet slips toward the apex; huge right atrium; heart fills the chest
core concept: Ebstein anomaly is apical displacement of the septal and posterior leaflets of the tricuspid valve from the AV junction, so part of the right ventricle becomes functionally atrial (atrialized right ventricle). The anterior leaflet is large and sail-like. In the four-chamber view the displacement between the mitral and tricuspid hinge points is markedly greater than the normal offset, and the right atrium, including the atrialized portion, is greatly enlarged. Color and spectral Doppler show severe tricuspid regurgitation, often with a jet originating deep in the ventricle. The heart is enlarged, with a raised cardiothoracic ratio, and a massive heart compresses the lungs, risking pulmonary hypoplasia. Severe regurgitation can prevent forward flow across the pulmonary valve (functional pulmonary atresia), and the ductus may fill the PA backwards; a circular shunt can develop. Tricuspid valve dysplasia, the main differential, has severe regurgitation without leaflet displacement. Postnatal Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome and tachyarrhythmias are common.
why it matters: Prognosis depends on heart size, tricuspid regurgitation severity, the presence of forward pulmonary flow and hydrops; severe fetal Ebstein has high mortality. Lithium exposure has a historical association, though the absolute risk is much smaller than once thought. Trap: functional pulmonary atresia can look like true PA/IVS; pulmonary regurgitation or improvement as RV pressure changes favors functional obstruction. Trap two: the abnormal displacement is measured in the four-chamber view, not the outflow view.
on the registry: Questions describe apical displacement of the tricuspid septal leaflet with a huge right atrium and ask for the diagnosis, teratogen or major complication.
checkpoint: Displaced septal leaflet plus giant RA equals Ebstein; dysplasia has no displacement

title: M-Mode and Doppler Rhythm Assessment
front clue: No ECG in utero: time the atrium and ventricle against each other
core concept: Fetal rhythm is diagnosed mechanically, by recording atrial and ventricular events together. With M-mode, the cursor is placed through an atrial wall and a ventricular wall (or the AV valve and a semilunar valve) at the same time, showing the sequence of atrial contraction (A) and ventricular contraction (V). With pulsed Doppler, a sample volume placed where mitral inflow and left ventricular outflow are adjacent shows the A wave of inflow followed by systolic outflow; alternative pairs include the SVC with ascending aorta, or a pulmonary vein with its neighboring pulmonary artery. The interval from the onset of the A wave to the onset of ventricular ejection is the mechanical PR (AV) interval, normally around 120 ms, with values above about 150 ms often taken as prolonged first-degree block. The normal fetal heart rate is about 110 to 160 bpm with a 1:1 AV relationship. Tissue Doppler and fetal magnetocardiography add timing detail in specialized centers.
why it matters: The core reasoning question for any arrhythmia is: what is the atrial rate, what is the ventricular rate, and how are they related? That one framework sorts PACs, SVT, flutter and heart block. Trap: an irregular rhythm without pause is not always ectopy; check for blocked beats. Trap two: in heart block, the atrial rate stays normal while the ventricular rate falls, so recording the ventricle alone hides the diagnosis. Use a fast sweep speed so intervals can be measured.
on the registry: Expect questions on where to place the M-mode cursor or Doppler gate to record AV relationships, and on the normal mechanical PR interval.
checkpoint: Atrial rate, ventricular rate, and their relationship sort every arrhythmia

title: Premature Atrial Contractions
front clue: The most common fetal irregularity: early atrial beats, usually benign
core concept: Premature atrial contractions (PACs, atrial ectopy) are the most common cause of an irregular fetal rhythm. On M-mode or Doppler an early atrial contraction is seen, followed by a ventricular contraction if conducted, then a pause before the next sinus beat. PACs may be conducted or blocked (nonconducted), when the early atrial beat arrives while the AV node is refractory; frequent blocked PACs in a bigeminal pattern produce an apparent bradycardia, often around 70 to 90 bpm, which must be differentiated from heart block by showing early, premature atrial beats rather than regular atrial activity. PACs often occur with a redundant or aneurysmal foramen ovale flap. Most resolve spontaneously before or soon after birth. A small proportion, commonly quoted as about 1 to 2 percent, develop sustained supraventricular tachycardia, so periodic heart rate checks, for example weekly or every one to two weeks, are commonly recommended.
why it matters: The skill tested is recognizing that blocked bigeminy is benign and must not be confused with complete heart block, which has a regular atrial rhythm and dissociated ventricular beats. Reasoning: in blocked PACs the atrial events are premature; in heart block they are regular. Trap: premature ventricular contractions are much less common and show an early ventricular beat without a preceding early atrial beat. Trap two: PACs without structural disease rarely need fetal echo follow-up beyond rate monitoring.
on the registry: Expect a scenario of an irregular rhythm with early atrial beats and questions on the diagnosis, the benign course, and the small risk of SVT.
checkpoint: PACs: common, benign, small SVT risk; blocked bigeminy mimics block

title: Supraventricular Tachycardia
front clue: Fixed rate above about 220 with 1:1 conduction; the risk is hydrops
core concept: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is the most common fetal tachyarrhythmia. The heart rate is typically about 220 to 300 bpm, often fixed with little variability, and atrial and ventricular contractions occur at a 1:1 ratio. The most common mechanism is AV reentry through an accessory pathway, which has a short VA interval (ventricle to next atrial contraction short compared with the AV interval). Long VA tachycardias, such as permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia and atrial ectopic tachycardia, are less common and often more resistant to treatment. SVT may be intermittent or sustained. Sustained tachycardia shortens diastolic filling, raises venous pressure and can lead to cardiac failure and hydrops within days. Sinus tachycardia, by contrast, is usually below about 200 bpm, varies, and points to maternal fever, infection, anemia or medications. Treatment is transplacental antiarrhythmic therapy given to the mother, such as digoxin, flecainide or sotalol, with maternal ECG monitoring; delivery may be considered near term.
why it matters: SVT is one of the few fetal conditions treated through the mother, and response is judged by fetal heart rate and resolution of hydrops. Reason from the rate and AV ratio: 1:1 at about 240 is SVT; atrial rate of about 450 with 2:1 conduction is flutter. Trap: hydrops reduces placental transfer of digoxin, so a hydropic fetus may need a different agent. Trap two: a heart rate of 180 with variability is not SVT.
on the registry: Expect questions with a fetal heart rate and AV ratio, asking for the diagnosis, mechanism, complication or treatment route.
checkpoint: 1:1 at about 240 bpm equals SVT; 2:1 with atria near 450 equals flutter

title: Atrial Flutter
front clue: Atria flutter near 400 to 500 while the ventricles follow at half the rate
core concept: Atrial flutter is a macro-reentrant circuit within the atria. The atrial rate is very fast, commonly about 300 to 500 bpm, and the AV node blocks some impulses, so the ventricular rate is lower, most often with 2:1 conduction giving a ventricular rate of about 220 to 250 bpm. Variable block (3:1, 4:1) can produce irregular ventricular rhythm. Diagnosis requires simultaneous assessment of atrial and ventricular activity, for example M-mode through the atrial wall and ventricle, which shows atrial contractions outnumbering ventricular contractions. Fetal atrial flutter usually presents in the third trimester and is rarely associated with structural heart disease, though it can occur with Ebstein anomaly or atrial enlargement. As with SVT, sustained flutter can cause heart failure and hydrops. Treatment is transplacental, with digoxin or sotalol commonly used. After birth, flutter often responds to electrical cardioversion and frequently does not recur.
why it matters: The trap is reading only the ventricular rate: a ventricular rate of 230 with flutter can be mistaken for SVT unless the atria are recorded. Count the atrial events in a single cycle on M-mode. Reason by AV ratio: more atrial beats than ventricular beats at a fast atrial rate equals flutter with block, while more atrial beats than ventricular beats at a normal atrial rate equals heart block. Gestational timing is a clue, because flutter clusters late in pregnancy.
on the registry: Questions provide atrial and ventricular rates and ask for the diagnosis, or ask which gestational period flutter typically appears in.
checkpoint: Atrial rate near 450, ventricles near 225: flutter with 2:1 block

title: Complete Heart Block
front clue: Atria at about 140, ventricles at about 60, marching independently
core concept: In complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block, no atrial impulses reach the ventricles. M-mode or Doppler shows a regular atrial rate in the normal range and a slower, regular, independent ventricular escape rate, typically about 40 to 80 bpm, with no fixed relationship. First-degree block is a prolonged mechanical PR interval, and second-degree block shows some atrial beats not followed by ventricular beats. About half of fetal complete heart block occurs with structural heart disease, chiefly left atrial isomerism and congenitally corrected transposition, and these structural cases carry a worse prognosis. Most isolated cases are caused by maternal autoantibodies, anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB, which cross the placenta and damage the conduction system, usually between about 16 and 26 weeks. The risk is about 1 to 2 percent in a first antibody-positive pregnancy and higher, roughly 15 to 20 percent, after a previously affected child. Antibodies can also cause myocarditis and endocardial fibroelastosis.
why it matters: Surveillance for antibody-exposed pregnancies is weekly or biweekly mechanical PR measurement in the window of risk, because first- and second-degree block may be partially reversible while complete block is generally permanent. Poor prognostic signs are ventricular rates below about 55 bpm, hydrops, ventricular dysfunction and endocardial fibroelastosis. Hydroxychloroquine is used to reduce recurrence risk. Trap: blocked atrial bigeminy also causes a slow ventricular rate but has premature, not regular, atrial beats. Trap two: heart block with complex structural disease suggests heterotaxy, not lupus.
on the registry: Expect a scenario of a mother with lupus or Sjogren antibodies and a fetal ventricular rate near 60, asking for the diagnosis, antibody or poor prognostic sign.
checkpoint: Anti-Ro plus fetal bradycardia with AV dissociation equals complete heart block
