title: Fetal Hydrops and CVP Score
front clue: Fluid in two or more compartments; score the heart, veins and arteries out of 10
core concept: Fetal hydrops is abnormal fluid in at least two fetal compartments: ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion or skin edema (commonly defined as skin thickness above 5 mm), often with polyhydramnios and placental thickening. Most hydrops today is nonimmune. Cardiovascular causes are among the most common, including structural defects with severe valve regurgitation, tachyarrhythmias, complete heart block, cardiomyopathy, cardiac tumors and high-output states such as anemia, arteriovenous malformations, sacrococcygeal teratoma and twin-twin transfusion. The cardiovascular profile (CVP) score, a 10-point score, assigns up to 2 points each to five categories: hydrops, venous Doppler (umbilical vein and ductus venosus), heart size (cardiothoracic area ratio), cardiac function (AV valve regurgitation, ventricular shortening, inflow pattern) and arterial Doppler (umbilical artery). A score of 10 is normal, and lower scores correlate with worse outcome. Signs of failure include cardiomegaly, holosystolic AV regurgitation, monophasic inflow, reversed DV a-wave and umbilical venous pulsations.
why it matters: Hydrops is the final common pathway of a failing fetal circulation, so the fetal echo goal is to find a treatable cause, especially tachyarrhythmia or anemia. Reasoning: high venous pressure appears first in the veins (DV a-wave, umbilical vein pulsations), then as effusions. Trap: an isolated pericardial effusion under about 2 mm can be normal and is not hydrops. Trap two: cardiomegaly with normal function may indicate high output, so check MCA peak systolic velocity for anemia.
on the registry: Expect items on the definition of hydrops, components of the CVP score and which cardiac causes are treatable in utero.
checkpoint: Hydrops equals two compartments; CVP score of 10 is normal

title: Myocardial Performance Index
front clue: Tei index: isovolumic times divided by ejection time; higher means worse
core concept: The myocardial performance index (MPI, Tei index) combines systolic and diastolic function in one Doppler measure. For the left ventricle, a sample volume placed to capture both mitral inflow and aortic outflow gives the isovolumetric contraction time (ICT), ejection time (ET) and isovolumetric relaxation time (IRT). MPI equals ICT plus IRT divided by ET. A modified method uses the valve clicks as landmarks to improve reproducibility. Normal fetal left ventricular MPI values are roughly 0.35 to 0.45, with slight change across gestation, and the index is relatively independent of heart rate and geometry. Rising MPI indicates dysfunction and is seen in the recipient twin of twin-twin transfusion syndrome, maternal diabetes, growth restriction and cardiomyopathy. Fetal cardiomyopathy may be dilated (large, poorly contracting ventricles with AV regurgitation, from infection, anemia, antibodies or genetic causes) or hypertrophic (thick walls, often from maternal diabetes). Shortening fraction from M-mode, normally about 28 percent or more, is another systolic index.
why it matters: MPI is valuable because the fetal heart is hard to measure by volume methods: there are no reliable fetal geometric assumptions and image quality varies. Reasoning: a sick ventricle takes longer to build and release pressure and ejects for a shorter time, so the ratio rises. Trap: MPI is a ratio of time intervals, so velocities and angle are less critical, but correct gate placement capturing both valve clicks is essential. Trap two: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of maternal diabetes usually regresses after birth.
on the registry: Questions ask for the MPI formula, whether an increased value is better or worse, and which conditions raise it.
checkpoint: MPI equals ICT plus IRT over ET; a rising MPI means worsening function

title: Indications for Fetal Echocardiography
front clue: Refer when the mother, the family or the fetus raises the risk
core concept: Fetal echocardiography is a detailed cardiac examination performed when the risk of congenital heart disease is higher than the general population baseline of roughly 1 percent of live births. Maternal indications include pregestational diabetes (type 1 or 2), phenylketonuria with poor control, autoimmune antibodies (anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB), exposure to teratogenic drugs, pregnancy by assisted reproductive technology, rubella in early pregnancy and maternal congenital heart disease. Family indications include congenital heart disease in a first-degree relative of the fetus, such as a parent or sibling, or a known genetic syndrome. Fetal indications are the strongest predictors: a suspected heart abnormality on screening, abnormal heart rate or rhythm, an extracardiac anomaly (such as omphalocele, diaphragmatic hernia, esophageal atresia or renal anomalies), a known or suspected chromosomal abnormality, nuchal translucency of 3.5 mm or more, hydrops or effusions, and monochorionic twins.
why it matters: A suspected abnormality on routine screening is the highest-yield indication, because most affected fetuses come from low-risk pregnancies with no identifiable risk factor. That is why the screening four-chamber, outflow and three-vessel views matter so much. Trap: gestational diabetes diagnosed after the first trimester does not carry the same structural risk as pregestational diabetes. Trap two: monochorionic twins are an indication even without other findings, because of higher structural risk and the cardiac effects of twin-twin transfusion.
on the registry: Expect questions asking which scenario is a fetal echo indication, or which indication carries the highest yield.
checkpoint: Suspected defect on screening is the strongest indication; NT of 3.5 mm or more qualifies

title: Maternal Diabetes and Teratogens
front clue: Poor sugar control in early pregnancy, plus certain drugs, increases heart defects
core concept: Pregestational diabetes is one of the most important maternal risk factors. Hyperglycemia during cardiac development, roughly the first 8 weeks, raises the risk of congenital heart disease several-fold, with risk rising with elevated HbA1c around conception. Associated lesions include conotruncal anomalies (transposition, DORV, truncus, tetralogy), VSD, heterotaxy and caudal regression. Later in pregnancy, poorly controlled diabetes can cause fetal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with a thickened septum and ventricular walls, which may obstruct the left ventricular outflow and usually regresses after birth. Teratogens linked to heart disease include retinoids such as isotretinoin (conotruncal and arch anomalies), anticonvulsants such as valproate and phenytoin, lithium (historically Ebstein anomaly, with a small absolute risk), alcohol (septal defects) and uncontrolled maternal phenylketonuria (tetralogy, coarctation, VSD). Third-trimester nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as indomethacin can constrict the ductus arteriosus, causing tricuspid regurgitation and right ventricular dysfunction.
why it matters: Separate early-pregnancy structural risk from late-pregnancy functional effects: diabetes causes both, at different times. NSAID ductal constriction is a classic functional question, because it is reversible when the drug is stopped. Trap: gestational diabetes beginning after organogenesis is not a strong structural risk factor, although it can still cause hypertrophy. Trap two: rubella classically causes patent ductus and branch pulmonary artery stenosis, not conotruncal lesions. Always ask when the exposure occurred relative to cardiac organogenesis before linking it to a structural defect.
on the registry: Expect questions pairing an exposure with its typical lesion, or asking about septal hypertrophy in a diabetic pregnancy and ductal constriction from NSAIDs.
checkpoint: Early sugar makes defects; late sugar thickens the septum; NSAIDs narrow the duct

title: 22q11.2 Deletion and Turner Syndrome
front clue: Conotruncal plus small thymus suggests 22q11; coarctation plus hygroma suggests Turner
core concept: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge or velocardiofacial syndrome) is the most common microdeletion associated with congenital heart disease. It predominantly causes conotruncal and arch anomalies: interrupted aortic arch type B (with the highest rate of deletion, around half), truncus arteriosus (roughly a third), tetralogy of Fallot, especially with pulmonary atresia or absent pulmonary valve, and right aortic arch or aberrant subclavian artery. Thymic hypoplasia or absence is an important clue, assessed anterior to the great vessels in the three-vessel view. Diagnosis requires chromosomal microarray or FISH, as standard karyotype misses the deletion. Turner syndrome (45,X) is associated with left-sided obstructive lesions: coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve are classic, along with hypoplastic left heart and partial anomalous pulmonary venous return. Turner fetuses often have a large septated cystic hygroma, lymphedema and hydrops. Noonan syndrome is linked to dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
why it matters: Genetic association questions are pattern matching by lesion family. Learn three anchors: cushion defects with trisomy 21, conotruncal with 22q11, left obstruction with Turner. Then adjust for clues such as a small thymus or a cystic hygroma. Trap: a normal karyotype does not exclude 22q11 deletion; microarray is needed. Trap two: transposition of the great arteries is a conotruncal lesion with a low rate of 22q11 deletion, so do not overapply the rule.
on the registry: Expect questions matching a lesion with its syndrome, or asking which test is needed to detect a 22q11 microdeletion.
checkpoint: 22q11 equals conotruncal and arch; Turner equals coarctation and bicuspid valve
ai_review_note: corePiece (low): Interrupted aortic arch type B is usually quoted with a 22q11 deletion rate of about 50 to 80 percent, so 'around half' understates the strongest association.

title: Heterotaxy Syndromes
front clue: Isomerism: two right sides with asplenia or two left sides with polysplenia
core concept: Heterotaxy (situs ambiguus) is abnormal arrangement of the thoracic and abdominal organs that is neither normal nor mirror image, usually with complex heart disease. Right atrial isomerism (asplenia pattern) gives bilateral morphologic right atria and is associated with severe lesions: unbalanced AVSD, single ventricle, pulmonary stenosis or atresia, transposition or DORV, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return. Abdominal clues include the aorta and IVC lying on the same side of the spine, with the IVC anterior (juxtaposition). Left atrial isomerism (polysplenia pattern) gives bilateral morphologic left atria and is associated with interrupted IVC with azygos continuation, seen as a dilated azygos vein running beside and behind the aorta (the double vessel sign), along with AVSD, left outflow obstruction and congenital complete heart block, sometimes with hydrops. Both forms may show a stomach and heart apex on opposite sides, a midline liver, bilateral SVC and atrial appendages that look alike.
why it matters: Heterotaxy is a reasoning chain: an abdominal situs abnormality predicts the heart lesion type. IVC and aorta on the same side points to right isomerism and severe cyanotic disease; an azygos vessel behind the aorta with bradycardia points to left isomerism. Prognosis is generally worse for right isomerism, but left isomerism with heart block and hydrops is also poor. Trap: heart block in heterotaxy is structural and not antibody related. Trap two: asplenia raises later infection risk.
on the registry: Expect items pairing findings such as an interrupted IVC with azygos continuation or a juxtaposed aorta and IVC with the correct isomerism.
checkpoint: Right isomerism: IVC and aorta together; left isomerism: azygos plus heart block

title: Cardiac Rhabdomyoma
front clue: Bright, round, multiple ventricular masses: think tuberous sclerosis
core concept: Rhabdomyoma is the most common fetal cardiac tumor. It appears as one or, more often, multiple homogeneous, well-circumscribed, echogenic masses within the ventricular myocardium or interventricular septum, sometimes in the atria. Tumors are usually first seen in the second or third trimester, may grow during pregnancy into the third trimester, and typically regress after birth. A strong association exists with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC1 or TSC2 genes): a large majority of fetuses with multiple rhabdomyomas have tuberous sclerosis, and the risk is high even with a single tumor. Fetal brain MRI looks for cortical tubers and subependymal nodules, and genetic testing and family evaluation are offered. Complications include inflow or outflow obstruction, arrhythmias (including Wolff-Parkinson-White after birth), ventricular dysfunction and hydrops. Other fetal cardiac tumors are rarer: teratoma is usually intrapericardial with a pericardial effusion, and fibroma is typically single, large, within the ventricular wall and may calcify.
why it matters: The prognosis for the heart is usually good because rhabdomyomas regress, but the long-term outcome is driven by tuberous sclerosis in the brain, with seizures and developmental problems. That is why the associated neurologic workup matters. Reasoning: multiple tumors make TSC almost certain. Trap: confusing a rhabdomyoma with an echogenic intracardiac focus; the focus is tiny, stable and on the papillary muscle. Trap two: a mass with a large pericardial effusion suggests teratoma rather than rhabdomyoma.
on the registry: Expect questions describing multiple echogenic ventricular masses and asking for the tumor type, associated syndrome or recommended additional imaging.
checkpoint: Multiple echogenic ventricular masses mean rhabdomyoma and tuberous sclerosis

title: Optimal Timing of Fetal Echo
front clue: 18 to 22 weeks is the sweet spot; earlier is possible, later may be needed
core concept: The standard fetal echocardiogram is usually performed at about 18 to 22 weeks of gestation, when the heart is large enough for detailed views, bone shadowing from ribs and spine is still limited and amniotic fluid is ample. Early fetal echocardiography, at about 12 to 16 weeks, usually transvaginally or with a high-frequency transabdominal probe, can identify major defects in high-risk pregnancies such as those with increased nuchal translucency, but detail is limited and a follow-up mid-trimester study is recommended. Beyond about 28 to 30 weeks, imaging becomes harder because of ossification, reduced relative fluid and a fetus that is more often spine anterior. However, some lesions are progressive or appear late, including coarctation, aortic and pulmonary stenosis evolving toward atresia, ventricular hypoplasia, ductal constriction, cardiac tumors, cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias, so third-trimester follow-up is often needed. Maternal obesity, prior abdominal surgery and fetal position also affect image quality and may require rescheduling.
why it matters: A normal midtrimester fetal echo does not guarantee a normal heart at birth, because several lesions evolve. Reasoning: obstructive lesions reduce flow, and reduced flow reduces chamber and vessel growth, so hypoplasia appears with time. Trap: ordering a first fetal echo at 32 weeks for a diabetic mother misses the best window. Trap two: a fetus lying spine up at the top of the image produces acoustic shadowing over the heart; waiting or having the mother change position often helps.
on the registry: Expect questions on the ideal gestational age window and which lesions may evolve after a normal midtrimester study.
checkpoint: 18 to 22 weeks is ideal; obstructive lesions can still evolve later

title: Image Optimization for the Fetal Heart
front clue: Small, fast target: zoom in, narrow the sector and keep the frame rate high
core concept: The fetal heart is small and beats about twice as fast as an adult heart, so temporal and spatial resolution both matter. Use the highest transducer frequency that gives adequate penetration. Zoom or magnify so the heart fills about a third to a half of the display, and narrow the sector width and reduce depth to raise the frame rate. Place a single focal zone at or just below the level of the heart, since more focal zones lower the frame rate. Keep persistence (frame averaging) low to avoid blurring fast-moving valves. A higher-contrast setting with a narrower dynamic range helps define the endocardium and septum against blood. Tissue harmonic imaging can improve images in patients with high body mass index, at some cost to resolution. Insonate septal structures perpendicular to the beam to avoid dropout, and use cine loop review frame by frame to evaluate valve motion and septal integrity. Patience with fetal position, and a sweep from abdomen to upper mediastinum, form the backbone of a systematic examination.
why it matters: Reasoning: each optimization trades one resolution for another. More focal zones and wider sectors improve coverage but lower frame rate, which matters more in a heart beating 140 times a minute. Trap: high persistence makes a moving valve look thick or blurred. Trap two: a false septal defect from dropout disappears when you change the angle of insonation. Questions frequently ask which control improves temporal resolution, and the answers are narrower sector, less depth, fewer focal zones and lower line density.
on the registry: Expect questions asking which control change increases frame rate or reduces artifact in fetal cardiac imaging.
checkpoint: Narrow, shallow, one focus, low persistence: high frame rate for a fast heart

title: Color and Spectral Doppler Settings
front clue: Match the color scale to the vessel; keep the box small and the angle low
core concept: Color Doppler is essential to fetal echo for detecting flow direction, shunts, regurgitation and stenosis. Set the velocity scale (pulse repetition frequency) to the target: a low scale, roughly 10 to 30 cm/s, for pulmonary veins, venous return and shunts across septal defects, and a higher scale, roughly 50 to 80 cm/s or more, for outflow tracts and valves, to avoid excessive aliasing. Keep the color box as small as practical, because a large box lowers the frame rate. Set color gain just below the level where random noise speckles appear, and keep the wall filter low for low-velocity flow. Align flow as close to parallel with the beam as possible. For spectral Doppler, use a small sample volume (about 1 to 3 mm) at the precise site, keep the angle of insonation below about 20 to 30 degrees with minimal angle correction, and use a fast sweep speed for timing. Aliasing is a clue to high velocity, such as a stenotic valve or the ductus venosus inlet.
why it matters: Doppler settings decide whether real flow is seen and false flow avoided. Reasoning: a scale set too high hides low-velocity shunts and pulmonary veins, while a scale too low causes aliasing that mimics turbulence. Trap: excessive color gain bleeds over the septum and can hide a VSD or create a false one. Trap two: power Doppler is more sensitive to slow flow but does not display direction. High-definition or directional power modes can help with small vessels.
on the registry: Expect questions on the appropriate color scale for pulmonary veins versus outflow tracts, and how to reduce aliasing or color bleeding.
checkpoint: Low scale for veins and shunts, high scale for outflows, small box

title: STIC and 4D Imaging
front clue: One slow sweep, many heartbeats, rebuilt into a single beating volume
core concept: Spatiotemporal image correlation (STIC) is an automated volume acquisition in which the transducer sweeps slowly across the fetal chest, usually over about 7.5 to 15 seconds with a sweep angle of roughly 20 to 40 degrees, collecting many cardiac cycles. Software detects the fetal heart rate from tissue motion and reorganizes the frames into a single volume representing one complete cardiac cycle that can be played as a loop. The volume can be displayed in multiplanar mode, as tomographic ultrasound imaging (parallel slices similar to CT), or as rendered views, and can be combined with color, power or high-definition flow. Advantages include offline review of all standard planes from one acquisition, sharing with remote experts and teaching. Best results come with the fetus still, spine posterior, and the four-chamber view as the starting plane. Artifacts arise from fetal movement, maternal breathing, irregular rhythm and acoustic shadowing; a motion artifact looks like discontinuity in the reconstructed planes.
why it matters: STIC is an adjunct, not a replacement: a poorly acquired volume cannot produce better information than the original 2D image. Reasoning: the reconstruction assumes a regular rhythm and a still fetus, so arrhythmias and movement break it. Trap: STIC is not a real-time method; the rebuilt cycle is a composite of many beats. Trap two: acquisition settings are chosen before sweeping; slow sweeps give better spatial resolution but are more vulnerable to motion.
on the registry: Expect questions on what STIC stands for, how the volume is built and which conditions cause artifacts.
checkpoint: STIC equals one automated sweep, many beats, one composite cycle

title: ALARA in Fetal Imaging
front clue: Watch TI and MI; Doppler outputs most; keep dwell time short
core concept: ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable) means obtaining diagnostic information with the least acoustic exposure. The output display shows the thermal index (TI), which estimates potential tissue temperature rise, and the mechanical index (MI), which estimates potential for nonthermal effects such as cavitation. For obstetric scanning, TIS (soft tissue) is generally monitored early in pregnancy, before significant bone ossification, commonly before about 10 weeks, and TIB (bone) afterward, because the fetal skeleton absorbs energy. Keeping TI at or below about 0.7 is a widely used goal, with shorter exposure times as TI increases. Pulsed spectral Doppler delivers the highest temporal average intensity, followed by color Doppler and then gray-scale. Practical steps include reducing output power and raising receiver gain instead, limiting dwell time over one spot, freezing the image while explaining findings, and avoiding unnecessary Doppler in the first trimester. Use of ultrasound only for medical indications and avoidance of nonmedical keepsake imaging follow the same principle.
why it matters: Fetal echo uses more Doppler than routine scans, so safety knowledge is tested directly. Reasoning: heating depends on intensity and time, and bone absorbs most energy, so TIB matters once the skeleton ossifies. Trap: increasing receiver gain does not increase patient exposure, whereas increasing output power does. Trap two: MI is linked to cavitation and gas bodies and is less relevant in the fetus, which has no air, but should still be kept low.
on the registry: Expect questions on which index to monitor at each gestational age, which mode has the highest output, and which control reduces exposure.
checkpoint: Lower power, raise gain, shorten dwell; TIB after early pregnancy, keep TI near 0.7 or lower
